text: Alex Pro argues that a representative three-neighborhood pilot reduced commute time by twelve percent, while explicitly making the conclusion probabilistic and conditional on service frequency.
Casey Con replies that unusually high existing ridership makes citywide generalization uncertain even if the pilot result is accurate.
Alex Pro answers that a staged rollout and six-month checkpoint directly test representativeness before lower-density expansion.
Casey Con argues that capital is committed before the test and proposes leasing vehicles to reduce sunk-cost risk.
Alex Pro answers that leasing costs more and a resale clause protects purchase economics unless cancellation is substantially more likely.
Casey Con replies that the resale clause excludes charging equipment and returns at most sixty percent, leaving the sunk-cost component incomplete.
Alex Pro argues that two-year savings exceed unrecovered capital but conditions the conclusion on the ridership forecast and checkpoint.
Casey Con concedes improvement while arguing that the same sample limits the forecast and supports only a limited experiment.
